title: Deep time: how the land was made
intro: Before there were people, the land itself moved. This chapter covers about 600 million years in a few minutes: the continents gather and break apart, a rift opens into West Africa and stops, the Niger Delta grows, volcanoes rise, the Sahara is born, and it turns green and dries again. If those 600 million years were one day, everything since the first Nok farmers would fit into its last half-second.
method: The continents are drawn where a published plate model puts them (Merdith et al. 2021), on a globe with the grid of latitude and longitude of the time. The outlines are today's continents with their shelves, simplified, so they show where the land was, not the coastlines of the time. Rocks record how far from the poles they formed but not how far east or west, so the longitudes of deep time are the model's choice. The last four scenes are on the plain map of today's land, lakes and rivers. A volcano is one cone symbol for every volcano or volcanic field. The glow, smoke, sand, grass and moving water drawn over the map are decoration, not measurements.

features.name: Where Nigeria is today
features.what: A marker for the rock that is now central Nigeria, so it can be followed as its plate moves. Nigeria itself dates from 1914.
features.location: A point in central Nigeria, moved with its plate.

features.name: Africa
features.what: The land that became Africa, including the rock under today's Nigeria.
features.location: Today's outline, moved by the plate model.

features.name: South America
features.what: Joined to Africa inside Gondwana. Their facing coasts still fit together.
features.location: Today's outline, moved by the plate model.

features.name: Antarctica
features.what: Part of Gondwana, beside southern Africa.
features.location: Today's outline, moved by the plate model.

features.name: India
features.what: Part of Gondwana until it broke away and drifted north.
features.location: Today's outline, moved by the plate model.

features.name: Australia
features.location: Today's outline, moved by the plate model.

features.name: North America
features.what: Joined to north-west Africa in Pangaea until the Central Atlantic opened between them.
features.location: Today's outline, moved by the plate model.

features.name: Europe and Asia
features.location: Today's outline, moved by the plate model.

features.name: Benue Trough
features.what: A rift about 1,000 km long and 150 km wide, from the Bight of Benin north-east to Lake Chad. It is the arm of a three-armed rift that stopped opening while the other two became the South Atlantic. The Benue River runs along it today.
features.location: A line through Abakaliki, Makurdi and the upper Benue near Numan to Lake Chad, following the source's description. The trough's mapped edges and its two upper arms are not drawn.

features.name: Coal swamps of the Anambra Basin
features.what: Brackish marshes at the southern end of the trough, around 70 million years ago. Their plants became the coal of the Udi Hills around Enugu, first shipped to Britain by 1914.
features.location: Placed at Enugu State's coordinates, near the Udi Hills where the coal is mined. The swamps covered a wider area that is not drawn.

features.name: Niger Delta
features.what: Since the Eocene, which began about 56 million years ago, the Niger and Benue have carried sand and mud to the sea here. The delta has built out about 250 km to the south-west over the ocean floor, to some 300,000 km², with sediment more than 10 km thick. It sits where the arms of the old rift met.
features.location: A point on today's delta. The coast and rivers are drawn as they are today; when the delta began, the shore was further inland.

features.name: Lake Mega-Chad
features.reach_note: A disc of 330,000 km², the smaller of the two sizes given, centred on today's Lake Chad. The lake's real shoreline is not drawn.
features.what: In wet periods Lake Chad was far larger than today, and drained to the Benue and the Niger through the Mayo Kebbi.
features.disputed: Its size is given as about 330,000 km² in one source and about 400,000 km² in another.

features.name: Ethiopian flood basalts
features.what: Around 30 million years ago, floods of lava poured out here, most of them within about a million years, and built up the Ethiopian highlands. The eruptions are thought to mark hot rock rising from deep in the Earth, the Afar plume.
features.location: A point on the Ethiopian plateau. The lava covered a much wider area, which is not drawn.

features.name: Biu Plateau
features.what: A volcanic plateau in north-eastern Nigeria. Some geologists link its volcanoes to the Cameroon line to the south.
features.location: Placed at the town of Biu, on the plateau. The volcanic field is wider and is not drawn.

features.name: Mount Cameroon
features.what: The most active volcano of the Cameroon line, close to the sea. It erupted from its flanks in 1999 and 2000, when the lava came within about 200 m of the sea, and briefly in 2012.

features.name: Kilimanjaro
features.what: Three volcanic centres beside the East African Rift. Activity began about 2.5 million years ago at Shira and later moved east to Mawenzi and Kibo. Kibo, the summit cone, is dormant rather than extinct.

features.name: Nyiragongo
features.what: A volcano above the city of Goma, in the western branch of the East African Rift. Its lava is unusually runny: in 1977 it ran down the upper slopes at up to 60 km/h. In 2002 and 2021 lava reached Goma. Sources give different numbers of people killed and displaced, so none are given here.

features.name: Northern Chad Basin
features.what: Where wind-blown dune sand about 7 million years old was found: the oldest known sign of a desert in the Sahara.
features.location: A point in the northern Chad Basin, as the sources describe it. The find spot is not drawn; the dashed ring shows the uncertainty.

scenes.title: Africa inside Gondwana
scenes.text: About 600 million years ago, the rock that is now Nigeria lay inside a growing supercontinent called Gondwana. Between about 600 and 530 million years ago, mountain building welded its pieces together: South America, Africa, Antarctica, Arabia, India and Australia. Africa and South America sat side by side. Watch where Nigeria's rock goes from here.

scenes.title: Pangaea breaks up
scenes.text: Gondwana had joined the northern continents into one supercontinent, Pangaea. About 200 million years ago, huge volcanic eruptions marked the start of its break-up, and the Central Atlantic opened between north-west Africa and North America. Between about 180 and 160 million years ago, Africa and Antarctica began to part.

scenes.title: The South Atlantic opens
scenes.text: Then South America and Africa pulled apart like a zip opening from the south. The rift spread north from about 150 or 140 million years ago, and new ocean floor formed from about 135 to 130 million years ago. North of the equator, where Nigeria's coast is now, rifting began after about 120 million years ago and went on until about 100 million years ago.
scenes.disputed: Sources disagree on when the last land link broke: dinosaur footprints suggest some connection until about 120 million years ago, while rifting north of the equator went on until about 100 to 96 million years ago. The page shows the whole range.

scenes.title: A rift that stopped: the Benue Trough
scenes.text: As the two continents parted, a third arm of the rift opened into Africa: the Benue Trough, about 1,000 km long, from the Bight of Benin to Lake Chad. It began to open at the start of the Cretaceous, about 145 million years ago, then stopped while the other two arms went on to become the South Atlantic. About 84 million years ago it was squeezed and folded. The Benue River runs along it today.

scenes.title: Coal swamps
scenes.text: Around 70 million years ago, brackish marshes spread at the southern end of the trough, in the Anambra Basin. Their plants were buried and slowly became coal. It is the coal of the Udi Hills around Enugu, first shipped to Britain by 1914.

scenes.title: Fire from below: Africa's volcanoes

when.label: about 66 million years ago to today

when.label: about 66 million years ago to today

beats.text: In the west, a line of volcanoes runs from the Gulf of Guinea inland. Nigeria's Biu Plateau is linked to it, and Mount Cameroon is its most active volcano.

when.label: from about 66 or 52 million years ago: sources differ

beats.text: About 30 million years ago, floods of lava poured out in Ethiopia, most of them within about a million years, and built the Ethiopian highlands.
In the East African Rift, Kilimanjaro began to grow about two and a half million years ago.

scenes.text: Africa's volcanoes rise where its plates are stretching apart, or where hot rock wells up from deep inside the Earth. In the west, a line of volcanoes runs from the Gulf of Guinea inland. Nigeria's Biu Plateau is linked to it, and Mount Cameroon is its most active volcano. About 30 million years ago, floods of lava poured out in Ethiopia, most of them within about a million years, and built the Ethiopian highlands. In the East African Rift, Kilimanjaro began to grow about two and a half million years ago. In recent decades Mount Cameroon erupted in 1999, 2000 and 2012, and the runny lava of Nyiragongo reached the city of Goma in 2002 and 2021, killing people and forcing many to flee.
scenes.disputed: Sources give different starts for the volcanoes of the Cameroon line, from about 66 to about 52 million years ago, and different dates for Kilimanjaro's first activity. Death tolls for Nyiragongo's eruptions also differ, so none are given.

scenes.title: The Niger Delta grows

when.label: about 56 million years ago to today

scenes.text: From about 56 million years ago, at the start of the Eocene, the Niger and the Benue carried sand and mud to the sea where the arms of the old rift met. The delta has built out about 250 km to the south-west, over the ocean floor, and now covers some 300,000 km². Its sediment is more than 10 km thick, and it is still growing.

scenes.title: The Sahara is born
scenes.text: The Sahara has a beginning. Wind-blown dune sand about 7 million years old, found in the northern Chad Basin, is the oldest known sign of a desert there. Before that find, most geologists thought the desert was only 2 to 3 million years old. A later study links the drying to the shrinking of the Tethys Sea, between about 11 and 7 million years ago.
scenes.disputed: Not all researchers accept the early date or the Tethys explanation.

scenes.title: A green Sahara, then the desert returns
scenes.text: From about 14,500 years ago, stronger monsoon rains turned the Sahara green, with grassland, lakes and rivers, and Lake Chad grew into a vast Lake Mega-Chad. The rains weakened between about 6,000 and 5,000 years ago, in steps and at different times in different places. In the eastern Sahara, archaeology shows people leaving the drying desert for the Nile valley and moving south towards today's Sahel. South of Lake Chad, farming and herding villages spread from about 1800 BCE. Whether people from the drying desert moved there is not shown by the sources checked so far.
